At $2 million, one extra dollar adds $5,000 in tax

After the 2019 tax change, sales at exactly $1,999,999 rose from about one a year to 21. Sales at the round threshold fell, while nearby untaxed round prices kept their spikes.

By Pablo Loschi1 October 2026Updated 15 November 20265 min readSources & methodsAlso on Housing Notes

A New York City home priced at $1,999,999 sits one dollar below a costly cliff. Under buyer transfer-tax rules introduced in 2019, hitting $2,000,000 adds roughly $5,000 to the tax bill—because the higher rate applies to the entire purchase price, not just the extra dollar.

What this means for a buyer

Near a New York threshold, a one-dollar bump in contract price can trigger thousands in tax. Always check the full rate schedule below (historical buyer mansion and supplemental rates shown here; other closing costs sit outside the example).

After the 2019 change took effect, recorded prices began stopping just short of the line. Sales at exactly $1,999,999 jumped from four in January 2016–March 2019 to 127 in 2020–2025 across the city's residential records.

Those two periods differ in length, so a fairer test compares each exact price with the sales around it. Before the reform, sales at exactly $2 million were 7.8 times the surrounding density. Afterward, the ratio was 2.3.

The cost of crossing the line

For a wholly residential purchase without an exemption, the buyer's mansion tax and supplemental tax total $19,999.99 at a price of $1,999,999. At $2 million, they total $25,000. Other taxes and closing costs sit outside this illustration.

The supplemental tax took effect on July 1, 2019, with a grandfathering rule for certain earlier contracts. The comparison leaves out the transition period and starts the later sample in January 2020.

Both sides of a deal have a reason to settle just under the line. The records show prices moving there after the reform; they cannot show what was said in any one negotiation.

Interactive illustration · historical 2019 rules

Original $2 million graphic and downloads

What happened at other round prices?

Round prices attract transactions even without a tax threshold. Before 2019, exactly $2 million and exactly $3 million were prominent price points. The reform made both the first dollar of a higher buyer-tax tier.

The spike at $3 million also fell, from 7.0 times the surrounding density to 2.5. Nearby round prices that did not become thresholds behaved differently. The ratio at $1.5 million rose from 4.9 to 5.8, and the ratio at $2.5 million rose from 6.7 to 10.0.

The $1 million threshold, which already existed, is another check: its ratio stayed at about 0.1 in both periods. Together, these comparisons separate the response at the new tax lines from a general change in how often buyers settle on round numbers.

The paper also tracks year-by-year shifts and splits houses from condominiums: the drop starts right with the 2019 reform and holds when foreclosure and lender transfers are excluded.

Who still pays for the extra dollar?

Across the new $2 million, $3 million and $5 million lines, exact-price sales fell by roughly 60% after 2019—leaving roughly four in ten exact-price sales at $2 million still paying $5,000 to $37,500 more than a contract price one dollar lower.

Notably, exact-price sales dropped less when the seller was a company—about 40%, versus 67% for individual sellers in the corrected linked sample—likely reflecting developer pricing schedules or contract conventions, though deeds do not record private negotiations.

Reading a comparable near $2 million

A sale at $1,999,999 may simply be stepping cleanly under a tax line. Anyone pulling comparables still has to inspect property details and terms, since public files omit concessions or credits.

I would welcome accounts from appraisers, brokers and buyers who have dealt with this boundary. Write to me about what happened at the table; identifying details need not be included.

An extra tax for buyers who need a mortgage

Borrowers face a separate mortgage recording charge on top of transfer taxes: applying the standard borrower schedule to recorded loans gives average calculated charges of 1.41% of price for houses and 1.28% for condos before credits or CEMA adjustments (co-op share loans fall outside it). Compare a cash purchase with a $720,000 loan—though statutory rules alone do not reveal how much of the cost buyers versus sellers ultimately absorb.

What a different tax schedule would change

For the city, the lost tax revenue is tiny: moved sales sidestep about $1.6 million to $2.9 million a year, under 1% of the $296 million implied by the 2019 schedule.

A marginal "slice" schedule—charging each rate only on the dollars above a threshold, like England’s 2014 stamp duty overhaul—eliminates every one-dollar cliff. Holding 2020–2025 sales fixed, the paper constructs two slice schedules that match the $296 million benchmark without cliffs, leaving only 7% of high-end sales paying slightly more under the progressive version (actual revenue would naturally shift once deals re-price).
